animism>aristotle.note: Aristotle's hylomorphism is documented; calling it animist is Bach's interpretation, not a standard historical classification.

plato>aristotle.note: Aristotle criticised the Forms and offered hylomorphic forms to salvage much of Plato's theory.

logos>christianity.note: Gospel of John identifies Christ as the incarnate Logos; John 1:1 quoted.

genesis>christianity.note: Old Testament is based primarily on the Hebrew Bible, with differences in order and contents.

aristotle>aquinas.note: Aquinas sought to synthesize Aristotelian philosophy with the principles of Christianity.

christianity>aquinas.note: Listed under Scholasticism; Summa is a guide to Catholic theology.

descartes>occasionalism.note: Motivated by dualist mind-body problem; associated with Descartes' Cartesian followers, notably Malebranche. Doctrine itself is older (al-Ghazali).

descartes>leibniz.note: Leibniz opposed Cartesian substance dualism and found Descartes' interactionism unintelligible.

descartes>empiricism.note: Innatism tied to Descartes; Locke is named the main antagonist of innate ideas.

empiricism>idealism.note: Berkeley responded to Locke; his approach to empiricism was later called subjective idealism.

empiricism>kant.note: Kant credited Hume with awakening him from a dogmatic slumber, then countered Hume's empiricism.

enlightenment>kant.note: Kant's 1784 essay: 'Sapere aude' as the motto of enlightenment.

enlightenment>utilitarianism.note: Bentham systematized utility and felicific calculation, but the broad Enlightenment-to-utilitarianism link is not explicitly stated on the checked page.

kant>hegel.note: Hegel and others after Kant built upon and challenged Kant's work.

idealism>hegel.note: Hegel's absolute idealism; Spirit comes to fully comprehend its own freedom.

darwin>dawkins.note: Proponents say it completes and extends Darwin; Mayr called the gene-as-object view non-Darwinian.

darwin>groupsel.note: Darwin made the first suggestion of group selection in The Descent of Man.

darwin>edelman.note: Named after Darwin; selectionist theory of neuronal groups.

celltheory>levin.note: No source found tying Levin's work to cell theory; cell theory does not treat cells as cooperating agents.

epiphenomenalism>chalmers.note: SEP's epiphenomenalism entry discusses Chalmers 1996 and the hard problem.

brentano>husserl.note: Brentano's intentionality and descriptive psychology were inherited and developed by Husserl's phenomenology.

brentano>freud.note: Freud is listed among Brentano's students at Vienna.

kant>husserl.note: Kant influenced Husserl, who recast phenomenology as transcendental idealism.

husserl>embodied.note: Husserl, Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty named as inspiration for the embodiment thesis.

cantor>russell.note: Russell found the paradox while examining Cantor's proof that there is no greatest cardinal.

frege>russell.note: Russell wrote to Frege in 1902 showing the paradox in Frege's system.

peano>goedel.note: Theorems apply to systems containing enough arithmetic, with Peano arithmetic the standard example.

russell>goedel.note: Goedel's 1931 paper demonstrated the incompleteness of the system of Principia Mathematica.

hilbert>goedel.note: Theorems are interpreted as showing Hilbert's program is impossible.

cantor>brouwer.note: Intuitionism created partly in reaction to Cantor's set theory; Brouwer rejected actual infinity.

leibniz>frege.note: Frege's motivation resembled Leibniz's calculus ratiocinator; Frege denied having achieved that aim.

hilbert>turing.note: Turing's 1936 paper negatively answered Hilbert's Entscheidungsproblem, shortly after Church.

lambda>turing.note: Lambda-definable, general recursive and Turing-computable functions are equivalent.

turing>morpho.note: Turing turned to mathematical biology in 1951 and published the paper in 1952.

turing>hypercomputation.note: Models computing non-Turing-computable functions; Turing's own 1938 oracle machines were the first.

turing>quantumcomp.note: Quantum computers add no computability power and can be simulated by a Turing machine.

shannon>dartmouth.note: Shannon was one of the four organizers and proposal authors.

vonneumann>conway.note: Page traces cellular automata to Ulam and von Neumann, then Conway's experiments with such rules.

digital>wolfram.note: Page presents Wolfram's A New Kind of Science and hypergraph project as part of digital physics.

digital>thooft.note: Page calls 't Hooft's cellular automaton interpretation the most technically developed contemporary version.

everett>deutsch.note: Page says Deutsch is a proponent of the many-worlds interpretation; 'leading' is the map's wording.

quantumcomp>deutsch.note: Deutsch's 1985 paper described the universal quantum computer.

mcculloch>cybernetics.note: McCulloch chaired the Macy cybernetics conferences; Pitts also attended.

mcculloch>pdp.note: Page dates connectionism's first wave to McCulloch and Pitts (1943).

cybernetics>gaia.note: Page describes Gaia as a cybernetic feedback system maintaining homeostasis.

schroedinger>friston.note: Friston co-authored 'Answering Schrödinger's question: a free-energy formulation' (2018), later than the point's date range.

dartmouth>minsky.note: Minsky was one of the four organisers, counted among the founding fathers of AI.

dartmouth>symbolic.note: Page says the rise of symbolic methods was initiated or encouraged by the workshop.

skinner>chomsky.note: Chomsky published an influential critique of Verbal Behavior in 1959.

chomsky>fodor.note: Page says Fodor followed Chomsky on nativism and drew on him to model his theory of mind.

symbolic>fodor.note: Page links the symbol-system hypothesis to the computational theory of mind associated with Putnam and Fodor.

symbolic>cyc.note: Page treats Cyc as a hand-built commonsense knowledge base within symbolic AI.

symbolic>schank.note: Page covers Schank's scripts as part of symbolic AI's commonsense-knowledge work.

symbolic>cogarch.note: Page says the Carnegie Mellon symbolic tradition culminated in Soar; also covers ACT-R.

symbolic>dreyfus.note: Dreyfus's critique was directed at symbolic AI; he held that skills cannot be captured in formal rules.

symbolic>harnad.note: Harnad's abstract: symbols in a formal symbol system grounded only in other meaningless symbols.

symbolic>brooks.note: Page says Brooks's approach rejected symbolic AI's representations.

symbolic>searle.note: Searle's target is symbol processing: syntactic manipulation without semantics.

minsky>pdp.note: Rumelhart and colleagues claimed in 1986 to have overcome the problems Minsky and Papert raised.

ivakhnenko>deeplearning.note: Page calls Ivakhnenko and Lapa's 1965 method the first working deep learning algorithm.

pdp>deeplearning.note: Page: Rumelhart et al. popularised backpropagation in 1986, though they did not invent it.

boltzmannmachine>deeplearning.note: Hinton's 2006 deep belief networks stack restricted Boltzmann machines.

schmidhuber>deeplearning.note: Page covers the neural history compressor and the work leading to LSTM.

deeplearning>olah.note: Zoom In studies trained networks' features and circuits; universality is its third claim.

deeplearning>bitter.note: Page cites deep learning and convolutional networks as continuing the trend the essay describes.

mountcastle>hawkins.note: Mountcastle's cortical column is a basic element of Hawkins's framework.

morpho>nca.note: The paper names Turing's 1952 patterns among the examples that inspired it.

braitenberg>brooks.note: Paper on Brooks's subsumption architecture cites Braitenberg's Vehicles as the fullest demonstration of the behavioural paradigm.

brooks>embodied.note: Page cites Brooks among roboticists arguing intelligence needs sensorimotor connection to the world.

dreyfus>embodied.note: The source links embodiment to Heidegger and opposes cognitivism, but does not explicitly say embodied cognition took up Dreyfus's critique.

llm>shanahan.note: Shanahan et al., 'Role-Play with Large Language Models', dated 2023.

llm>butlin.note: Butlin et al. assess recent AI systems against indicator properties from theories of consciousness.

eliza>llm.note: Article calls ChatGPT a direct descendant of ELIZA and discusses users attributing human qualities to both.

agi>airisk.note: Page discusses whether AGI represents an existential risk, citing Bostrom.

functionalism>searle.note: Argument is explicitly directed against functionalism and computationalism.

functionalism>chalmers.note: Functional explanation leaves experience unexplained; Chalmers targets reductive functionalism only.

functionalism>thagard.note: Paper's title and abstract state it; Thagard says substrate independence fails in important real cases, not always.

functionalism>seth.note: Seth challenges computational functionalism and argues consciousness depends on our nature as living organisms.

functionalism>lerchner.note: Abstract offers a 'physically grounded refutation of computational functionalism'.

searle>seth.note: Seth credits Searle with biological naturalism but says he uses the term in a slightly different way.

qualia>nagel.note: Nagel's paper is often cited in qualia debates, though it does not use the word 'qualia'.

qualia>levine.note: Levine's explanatory gap argument is presented as an argument about qualia.

chalmers>panpsychism.note: The overview links panpsychism's revival to the hard problem and identifies Chalmers as treating it as viable.

mysterianism>chalmers.note: New mysterianism (McGinn) is treated as one response to the hard problem.

chalmers>illusionism.note: Frankish: 'the hard problem is replaced by the illusion problem'.

dennett>illusionism.note: Frankish coins the term and names Dennett as illusionism's pre-eminent defender.

dennett>chalmers.note: In The Conscious Mind (1996) Chalmers calls Dennett's position a denial of consciousness.

hofstadter>dennett.note: The page identifies Hofstadter and Dennett as co-editors and co-authors of The Mind's I.

goedel>hofstadter.note: Gödel's self-referential construction is Hofstadter's prototypical strange loop.

goedel>penrose.note: Penrose argued from Gödel's theorem to non-computability of mind; the argument is widely criticised.

quantumcomp>penrose.note: Penrose and Hameroff section discusses quantum coherence in microtubules and includes a quote contrasting them with nerve signals as quantum-computer material.

ncc>iit.note: Koch describes his NCC work with Crick and subsequent integrated-information work with Tononi.

binding>ncc.note: Crick and Koch (1990) tied binding to visual awareness via synchronous 40 Hz oscillations.

iit>aaronson.note: Aaronson showed simple arrangements of logic gates would have unboundedly high phi.

iit>tegmark.note: Abstract: the approach 'generalizes Giulio Tononi's integrated information framework' to arbitrary quantum systems.

panpsychism>iit.note: Chalmers and Searle consider IIT a form of panpsychism; Tononi and Koch accept only some elements.

gwt>bengio.note: Paper says the prior is inspired by and anchored on global workspace theory.

gwt>butlin.note: Global workspace theory is one of the theories from which indicator properties are derived.

hot>butlin.note: Computational higher-order theories are among the theories surveyed.

hot>ast.note: Graziano et al. argue AST and HOT are interlocking perspectives on the same mechanism.

minsky>gwt.note: Baars explicitly says GWT views the brain as a society of mind made of specialized, mostly unconscious processors.

freud>kahneman.note: The article explicitly compares Freud's unconscious primary process with Kahneman's largely unconscious System 1.

haidt>kahneman.note: Page says the rider and elephant metaphor corresponds to Systems 2 and 1.

friston>seth.note: Seth builds his case on predictive processing and the free energy principle; 'beast machines' phrase is used.

damasio>seth.note: Seth identifies Damasio's framework as related and grounds feeling and selfhood in interoception and physiological homeostasis.

james>damasio.note: Damasio 'recovered William James' perspective on feelings as a read-out of body states' and expanded it.

fields>levin.note: Levin's publication list shows more than a dozen Fields and Levin papers since 2018.

jaynes>westworld.note: The concept played a central role in Westworld; season 1 finale is titled 'The Bicameral Mind'.

idealism>hoffman.note: Hoffman acknowledges similar idealist ideas, then explicitly says MUI theory is not idealism.

metzinger>illusionism.note: Blackmore's illusionist account explicitly cites Metzinger when describing a temporary self-model of a continuing observer.

piaget>kegan.note: Kegan places his work in the constructive-developmental tradition that includes Piaget.

huxley>leary.note: The influence section says Leary found the book corroborated his psilocybin experience, arranged a meeting, and became friendly with Huxley.

pribram>penrose.note: The page discusses both Pribram's quantum-field holonomic theory and Penrose-Hameroff Orch-OR as quantum-mind proposals.

embodied>seth.note: Seth draws on autopoiesis (Maturana and Varela) and cites enactive and 4E work as allied to his view.

matrix>simulation.note: The Matrix popularised the idea of humans unknowingly living in a machine-generated reality.

egan>simulation.note: Egan's synopsis describes conscious software copies of brains running in virtual reality.

watts>illusionism.note: Blindsight treats consciousness as real but dispensable, which differs from illusionism; Watts's own notes cite Metzinger, and the novel predates the term.

cogarch>bach.note: Bach's dissertation devotes comparative sections to Soar and ACT-R and contrasts their scope with Psi/MicroPsi.

maslow>bach.note: Bach explicitly says Maslow's hierarchy of needs is better understood as a hierarchy of purposes.

bischof>bach.note: Bach states that Dörner's blueprint incorporates Bischof's ideas and discusses Bischof's cybernetic treatment of psychological feedback loops.

occ>bach.note: Bach explicitly contrasts OCC's implemented emotion categories with MicroPsi emotions emerging from whole-system modulator configurations.

sloman>bach.note: In the methodology section, Bach cites Sloman for understanding minds through the active design stance of a constructing engineer.

cybernetics>bach.note: At 22:47, Bach explains motivation cybernetically: needs are balanced by a homeostatic control system.

schank>bach.note: Bach cites Schank and Abelson for hierarchical scripts, then supplies a neural implementation for sensorimotor script execution.

minsky>bach.note: Bach describes Minsky's view in these terms and elsewhere calls him the most influential thinker on minds.

gwt>bach.note: In section 1, Bach lists Baars's GWT as a functional approach whose explanation converges on phenomenal consciousness.

ast>bach.note: Listed by Bach among perspectives converging on his own.

metzinger>bach.note: Bach says the self is a model, not an agent, and explicitly directs readers to Metzinger's Being No One.

dennett>bach.note: Bach explicitly calls Cortical Conductor Theory an extension of Dennett's multiple-drafts model.

kant>bach.note: No statement by Bach on Kant's phenomena/thing-in-itself was found; Kant work at CIMC is by colleagues.

plato>bach.note: At 1:26:49, Vervaeke calls Plato's cave the first simulation theory; Bach answers, “Almost.”

buddhism>bach.note: At 00:21:49, Bach says stage-six enlightenment is found mostly among advanced Buddhist meditators.

chalmers>bach.note: At 11:28–12:53, Bach calls Chalmers's hard problem a misunderstanding and explains experience as a mind-created world.

panpsychism>bach.note: At 37:23–37:54, Bach says physical things cannot be conscious; only suitable representational software structures can dream.

lucid>bach.note: In the daytime-dream passage, Bach says waking neocortical simulation uses dream circuitry but is constrained by sensory input.

levin>bach.note: At 38:03–38:36, Bach attributes to Levin the hypothesis that morphogenesis and mind use the same coherence algorithm.

sicp>bach.note: Bach and Sorensen quote this SICP opening in the CIMC hypothesis paper.

dawkins>bach.note: At 00:38–00:44, the discussion explicitly moves from Dawkins's gene competition to Bach's competing software agents.

greekgods>bach.note: At 2:36:30–2:36:54, Bach describes Greek gods as cross-mind psychological archetypes.

christianity>bach.note: Bach describes Christianity awakening as a societal agent, with the Catholic Church as its nervous system and brain.

jaynes>bach.note: Bach discusses gods as mental constructs and cross-mind selves, but no opened source tied this account to Jaynes.

digital>bach.note: Early in the talk, Bach says the universe produces regular patterns and therefore necessarily and sufficiently is a computer.

lamettrie>bach.note: Near the opening, Bach credits La Mettrie with humans as mathematical machines; elsewhere he calls computationalism the new mechanism.

cimc>lerchner.note: Page opened. Reply is by Sorensen and Hildebrandt-Harangozó, not Bach; Lerchner targets computational functionalism, not CIMC by name.

brouwer>bach.note: Bach strongly advocates constructive mathematics, but no opened source documented a specific debt to Brouwer or intuitionism.

cantor>bach.note: In the mathematics-foundations section, Bach starts with Cantor's sets, then rejects completed infinities as unconstructible.

hypercomputation>bach.note: Bach defends Church–Turing universality and doubts physical hypercomputers, but the categorical note is stronger than the opened passages.

wittgenstein>bach.note: Bach presents the Tractatus as Wittgenstein's attempt to reverse-engineer thought into a precise, formal language.

aquinas>bach.note: Bach explicitly derives faith, love, and hope as Aquinas's three divine virtues for forming a higher-level agent.

utilitarianism>bach.note: In the ethics section, Bach critiques utilitarian aggregation of hedonic states and derives ethics from negotiations among agents.

llm>bach.note: From 01:14 onward, Bach explains language models as representational-state transition functions, useful but ungrounded components of larger systems.

shanahan>bach.note: The event page lists Bach and Shanahan as featured speakers on the same machine-sentience panel.

turing>cimc.note: From the CIMC hypothesis paper (Bach and Sorensen).

butlin>cimc.note: Appendix B cites Butlin et al. while describing nonprofit research on AI moral patienthood and welfare.

bach>cimc.note: The Bach-authored essay grounds CIMC's hypothesis in computational functionalism, conductor theory, and consciousness arising near the beginning of development.

friston>cimc.note: Whitepaper Appendix A lists Karl Friston on the Scientific Advisory Board (page opened).

wolfram>cimc.note: Whitepaper Appendix A lists Stephen Wolfram on the Scientific Advisory Board (page opened).

iit>cimc.note: The whitepaper says IIT denies consciousness to a functionally perfect digital brain simulation when its hardware causal architecture differs.
